full_text:
दिल्ली में अगले 6 दिन तक गिरेगा तापमान, पढ़ें बदलते मौसम का अपडेट
Delhi Weather Update: IMD के अनुसार, सोमवार को दिल्ली में अधिकतम तापमान करीब 38.1 डिग्री सेल्सियस रहा, जो सामान्य से 3.2 डिग्री सेल्सियस अधिक रहा. वहीं, न्यूनतम तापमान 28.6 डिग्री सेल्सियस रहा.
दिल्ली-एनसीआर में मौसम का मिजाज एक बार फिर से बदलता हुआ नजर आ रहा है. सोमवार (27 जुलाई) को हुई बारिश ने शहर के लोगों को उमस भी गर्मी से बड़ी राहत दी है. भारतीय मौसम विभाग (IMD) के अनुसार, अगले 24 घंटों में अधिकतम तापमान में कोई खास बदलाव होने की संभावना नहीं है, लेकिन इसके बाद अगले 6 दिनों में शहर का अधिकतम तापमान 2-3 डिग्री सेल्सियस तक गिर सकता है.
IMD के अनुसार, सोमवार (27 जुलाई) को दिल्ली में अधिकतम तापमान करीब 38.1 डिग्री सेल्सियस रहा, जो सामान्य से 3.2 डिग्री सेल्सियस अधिक रहा. वहीं, न्यूनतम तापमान 28.6 डिग्री सेल्सियस, जो सामान्य से 1.3 डिग्री अधिक है. इस दौरान नमी का अधिकतम स्तर 100 प्रतिशत और न्यूनतम स्तर 51 प्रतिशत रहा.
पिछले 24 घंटों में हल्की बारिश से मिली राहत
पिछले 24 घंटों में दिल्ली में कुछ जगहों पर बहुत हल्की बारिश दर्ज की गई, जिससे लोगों को गर्मी और उमस से थोड़ी राहत मिली. इस दौरान दिल्ली के न्यूनतम और अधिकतम तापमान में 1-2 डिग्री सेल्सियस की बढ़ोतरी देखने को मिली है. पिछले 24 घंटों में दिल्ली में न्यूनतम तापमान 25-29 डिग्री सेल्सियस और अधिकतम तापमान 36-38 डिग्री सेल्सियस के बीच दर्ज किया गया. विभाग के अनुसार, पिछले 24 घंटों में सुबह 8:30 बजे तक बारिश नहीं हुई, लेकिन सुबह 8:30 बजे से शाम 5:30 बजे के बीच 8 मिमी बारिश दर्ज की गई. इस दौरान दक्षिण-पूर्वी दिशा से हवाएं चलीं, जिनकी गति 10 से 15 किलोमीटर प्रति घंटा रही.
अगले दो दिनों तक होगी बारिश
बात करें मंगलवार (28 जुलाई) के मौसम की तो IMD के अनुसार, आज आमतौर पर आसमान में बादल छाए रहने का अनुमान है. सुबह से दोपहर के बीच अधिकतर इलाकों में बहुत हल्की से हल्की बारिश और कुछ जगहों पर मध्यम बारिश के आसार हैं. शाम या रात के समय कई जगहों पर बहुत हल्की से हल्की बारिश और कुछ अलग-अलग इलाकों में मध्यम बारिश होने की संभावना है.
इस दौरान अधिकतम तापमान 32-34 डिग्री सेल्सियस और न्यूनतम तापमान 23-25 डिग्री सेल्सियस के बीच रहने का आनुमान है. विभाग ने आज मंगलवार और बुधवार के लिए दिल्ली-एनसीआर में येलो अलर्ट जारी किया है. इस दौरान 15-20 किमी प्रति घंटे की गति से सतही हवाएं चल सकती हैं, जो झोकों के साथ बढ़ भी सकती हैं.

A fourth heatwave of the year is now under way for parts of the UK, with temperatures expected to climb into the mid-30s Celsius later this week.
This latest spell of heatwave threshold-level temperatures is expected to peak on Wednesday in the south-east and east of England.
The UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) has warned the rising temperatures could increase health risks, particularly for vulnerable groups.
It has issued amber heat health alerts, external for much of eastern England that come into force on Wednesday.
North-south split
The heatwave will not be felt in all parts of the country, with clouds and outbreaks of rain continuing in Northern Ireland, Scotland and northern England.
The hot weather will be focused on central, southern and eastern England on Tuesday thought it may spread slightly northwards and westwards into midweek.
Temperatures in England and Wales are forecast to rise to around 25-32C for the next few days with Wednesday likely to see the peak, with readings of 30-35C across the Midlands, southern and eastern England.
Scotland and Northern Ireland will generally remain cooler and showery with temperatures in the high teens or low to mid-20s Celsius.
Current forecasts suggest that the intense heat across southern and central parts of the UK this week will be short-lived compared to the three previous widespread heatwaves this summer.
Some isolated showers may arrive later in the week.
Heat health alerts issued
July 2026 has been notably hot. The Met Office says the UK mean temperature so far this month is 17.5C, which currently makes it the second hottest of any month on record, behind only July 2006 (17.8C).
The ongoing heat means the East Midlands, East of England, London, and the South East are all under amber alerts heat health alerts from 09:00 on Wednesday until 09:00 Thursday.
The UKHSA warns that significant impacts are likely across health and social care services due to the high temperatures, especially as much of July has seen temperatures well above average by day and by night.
Yorkshire and the Humber, the West Midlands and the South West are all under less severe yellow alerts for the same period.
When will it rain?
An ongoing lack of rain means hosepipe bans are in force for millions of households and dry vegetation has provided fuel for wildfires to burn in a number of areas.
Though there was some rain this weekend, the driest locations - including central, southern and eastern England - saw little, if any, meaningful rainfall.
According to the Met Office, rainfall in England this month is at 4.4mm, one of the lowest levels on record, behind only February 1891 (3.3mm) and tied with June 1925 (4.4mm).
Rainfall levels in Wales, where drought was triggered last week in some parts, are so low that July 2026 is currently the fourth driest of any month since records began.
As this next spell of hot weather develops across England and Wales, the lack of significant rain means dry ground and low soil moisture levels are likely to become an increasing concern.
Wisley in Surrey has been one of the driest locations in south-east England with 40 days of no rain as of 27 July.
Though some isolated showers are expected later in the week, there is no significant rain in the forecast.

France is preparing for its fourth major heatwave of the year as soaring temperatures and prolonged drought continue to fuel one of the country’s worst wildfire seasons on record, with firefighters battling a massive blaze near Bordeaux that has already burned 42,000 hectares.
Temperatures in Bordeaux are expected to reach 33 degrees Celsius (91 degrees Fahrenheit) on Tuesday, around seven degrees above the historical average for the period between 1961 and 1990, according to the Reuters Climate Monitor. Weather officials warn temperatures could climb to 37 degrees Celsius (99 degrees Fahrenheit) on Wednesday, further increasing the risk of new fire outbreaks.
Macron Calls Wildfire Crisis Unprecedented
President Emmanuel Macron, who visited the affected region on Monday, described the crisis as the most severe France has faced in decades.
“The situation we are dealing with today is the most severe we have ever recorded, the toughest since the Second World War,” Macron said.
Firefighters managed to contain the blaze overnight, but authorities warned that strong winds, extreme heat and dry vegetation continue to threaten containment efforts.
“Everything will depend on how the firefighters on the ground get on,” Gironde Senator Nathalie Delattre told BFM TV on Tuesday.
Thousands Evacuated as Fire Continues to Spread
The wildfire is centered in the Landes region southwest of Bordeaux, where extensive pine forests have become highly combustible after months of dry conditions. Officials said the fire has already consumed approximately 42,000 hectares, making this France’s most destructive wildfire season since records began.
More than 220,000 people, including residents and holidaymakers, have been evacuated from affected areas as emergency services continue efforts to protect communities and infrastructure.
Conditions have improved in Biscarrosse, around 40 kilometers south of Bordeaux, where another major wildfire erupted last week. Local authorities have begun allowing approximately 15,000 evacuated residents and tourists to return home and reopen nearby campsites.
However, officials cautioned that the danger has not passed.
“The favorable development does not mean the risk has been eliminated,” local authorities said in a statement, warning that flare ups remain possible because of continued drought and changing wind conditions.
Heatwave Threat Continues
Meteorologists expect temperatures to continue rising across southwestern France through midweek, creating conditions that could rapidly accelerate existing fires or ignite new ones.
Analysis
France’s escalating wildfire crisis highlights how increasingly frequent and intense heatwaves are reshaping Europe’s climate risk landscape. The country has now experienced four major heatwaves in a single year, reflecting a broader pattern of prolonged drought, record temperatures and worsening fire conditions across southern Europe.
The scale of the Bordeaux wildfire demonstrates the growing difficulty of managing forests that have become significantly more vulnerable after successive years of extreme heat. Even when fires are contained, strong winds and persistently dry conditions create a high risk of flare ups, forcing authorities to maintain large scale evacuations for extended periods.
Beyond the immediate humanitarian impact, recurring wildfires carry significant economic consequences through damage to tourism, agriculture, forestry and public infrastructure. They also place growing pressure on emergency services that must respond to increasingly frequent climate related disasters.
As Europe continues to warm, governments are likely to face greater demands for investment in wildfire prevention, forest management and climate adaptation. The Bordeaux blaze underscores that extreme heat is no longer an isolated weather event but an increasingly persistent security, environmental and economic challenge.

France and Spain continued battling major wildfires Tuesday as rising temperatures, low humidity and shifting winds threatened to reignite flames and hamper containment efforts.
In southwestern France, the Gironde megafire remained stabilized but uncontrolled after burning 42,000 hectares (103,784 acres) since July 22, with no increase in the affected area overnight, according to local authorities.
Several flare-ups north of Le Porge and Cap-Ferret were brought under control, but Gironde Prefect Sophie Brocas warned that the situation remained "highly unpredictable," BFMTV reported.
Temperatures were forecast to reach 35C (95F) in Gironde and 37C (98.6F) in the neighboring Landes department, while changing wind directions could make the fire's behavior difficult to predict.
Around 2,750 firefighters, 1,500 military personnel, 1,440 members of the security forces and 18 aircraft were deployed to battle the blaze.
Lt. Col. Olivier Cravata of the Gironde Fire and Rescue Service said crews were seeking to secure the fire's perimeter before conditions deteriorated later in the day.
"We have 130 kilometers (81 miles) to deal with," he said.
Seven French departments were placed under an orange alert for a high risk of forest fires.
Volunteer firefighter Laurent Masson, 38, was killed "in the line of duty" when the fire engine he was driving skidded off the road in Bouches-du-Rhone. Four firefighters were slightly injured in a separate accident in the Var department.
In Spain, firefighters faced critical hours ahead of the country's fourth heat wave of the summer.
Fires have burned about 50,000 hectares in Avila, 28,000 in Madrid and 8,500 in Castellon. The total area burned nationwide has reached 172,400 hectares this year, according to public broadcaster RTVE.
More than 180,000 people remained evacuated or confined across Spain.
Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska described the Avila blaze as "the most significant and most aggressive fire in Spain's history."
More than 400 emergency personnel worked overnight to contain the Valdemaqueda fire in Madrid before southerly winds were expected to intensify.
Temperatures were forecast to reach 36-38C across much of Spain and exceed 40C (104F) in the Guadiana and Guadalquivir valleys.

full_text:
JACKSON, Miss. (WLBT) -Air conditioners are not built for the current level of extreme heat, according to HVAC technicians, who say most units are designed and tested to perform best at around 95 degrees.
At Environment Masters, an AC, plumbing and electric company, the phones have not stopped. Technicians said they walked in Monday morning to 100 calls already on the board.
“You walk into the building today on Monday and we’ve already got 100 calls laid out. Like, that’s how we’re starting the day. That’s 100 houses without air,” said Ben Nalty, Environment Masters General Manager.
Attic temps top 150 degrees
Beyond the volume of calls, technicians said working conditions have been severe. Attic temperatures on recent jobs have climbed past 150 degrees.
“We love to play superhero. We love to come help people. But you know, it does — it’s a toll on them,” Nalty said.
What you should — and should not — do
Technicians said one of the most common mistakes they see is homeowners cranking the thermostat down to the mid-60s in an attempt to cool the house faster.
“We just often see a lot of people that have that expectation of running it in the mid 60s. And that’s abusive at this point. If it’s going to be 99 degrees, that’s way beyond that 20 degree temperature differential, way beyond that design test set point,” noted Nalty.
Instead, Environment Masters recommends small, steady thermostat adjustments and basic maintenance steps: change the air filter and keep the outdoor unit clear of grass clippings and debris.
Residents adjust habits
Resident Regina Banks said she is mindful about avoiding large temperature swings on her unit.
“I tell anybody about living in Mississippi your whole life you can live here but still won’t get used to the weather,” Banks said.
Environment Masters said it is pacing crews for long shifts to work through the call volume.

Salvation Army Outreach Team Supports People During Extreme Heat
Throughout July, temperatures have frequently climbed above 30 C across Ontario. In Ottawa, The Salvation Army’s outreach team is supporting people experiencing homelessness by providing care during periods of extreme heat.
“Our Salvation Army teams are out on the road seven days a week. They’re out there all the time helping folks who are staying outside in this heat,” says Ty Von Boetticher, supervisor of outreach and housing services at The Salvation Army’s Ottawa Booth Centre.
We make sure those we serve are hydrated and let them know that we can take them to drop-in centres or shelters with air conditioning.”
During periods of extreme heat, outreach workers provide water and conversation, conduct wellness checks and transport clients to places where they can cool off.
“High temperatures can be very dangerous. So, we make sure those we serve are hydrated and let them know that we can take them to drop-in centres or shelters with air conditioning,” Ty adds. “We also keep an eye out for signs of heat stroke or exhaustion. We can refer clients to hospitals if needed.”
Transportation is available for people needing access to The Salvation Army’s shelter, drop-in centres or cooling spaces. The outreach team also offers medical assistance.
“We have a nurse practitioner who joins us on Mondays. She has been great and has been able to refer clients to more extensive medical care,” Ty adds.
While responding to the heat is a priority during the summer, the team’s work goes beyond this. Staff build relationships with the individuals they see daily and connect them with housing supports and community resources.
“We’re seeing more and more people having to sleep outside and not necessarily by choice.”
Ty says there is a noticeable rise in demand for shelter space, which has led to limited availability in the city.
“We’re seeing more and more people having to sleep outside and not necessarily by choice, but because they’re forced to,” he says.
Despite the growing need, Ty says the outreach program has expanded thanks to the support of the community and donors. He also adds that they take feedback from those they serve into account.
“We’re always looking to improve our program and we are especially open to suggestions that come from clients.”
The Salvation Army’s outreach team in Ottawa assists approximately 600 individuals across the city, including those living in encampments.
With support from the community, The Salvation Army can continue providing practical assistance to people experiencing homelessness.
By Juan Romero

Health experts said prolonged stretches of extreme heat give the body little time to recover, especially when overnight temperatures remain warm. That can lead to cumulative dehydration, increase the risk of heat-related illness, and make outdoor activities more dangerous.
“Part of the reason it’s more dangerous is there’s less recovery time,” said Dr. Cynthia Cross, a pediatric hospitalist at Le Bonheur Children’s Hospital. “Our houses don’t cool off the way they would if there were a break in the heat. We may be dehydrated already. And then with several days of heat, that just tends to get a bit worse.”
Dr. Cross said children are especially vulnerable because they lose fluids faster than adults and often don’t recognize the warning signs of dehydration or heat illness.
“Kids tend to dehydrate faster,” she said. “They also aren’t able to necessarily protect themselves or recognize the signs of heat-related illness.”
She said while the body gradually acclimates to hot weather, that doesn’t mean it’s protected from the effects of prolonged heat exposure.
“It takes a while for the body to get acclimated to the heat, to where we don’t tend to complain about it as much, but the effects of extreme heat exposure are still there,” Dr. Cross said.
Warm nights can make the problem worse because the body never fully cools down, she said.
“It doesn’t allow the body temperature time to come down, doesn’t allow you to recover,” Dr. Cross said. “There is an optimal temperature at which our bodies work best, and you may stay a bit hotter.”
Dr. Mark Castellaw, a family medicine physician with Baptist Medical Group, said many people become complacent after making it through the first few days of a heat wave.
“People get tired of staying inside, and they want to get back out and start doing normal activities," Dr. Castellaw said. “But when the weather is being like it has been, it’s putting yourself at extreme risk.”
He said people taking prescription medications, including blood pressure medications, diuretics, and some diabetes medications, face an even greater risk because they can become dehydrated more quickly or develop dangerous electrolyte imbalances.
“If you’re on any type of prescription medicine, blood pressure medicine, or diabetic medicines, this heat that we’re experiencing can absolutely be deadly,” Dr. Castellaw said.
Doctors said one of the first signs of dehydration is dizziness or feeling lightheaded. Other warning signs include fatigue, decreased urination, and unusual sleepiness in children. Confusion, a high body temperature, or stopping sweating are signs of a medical emergency that require immediate care.
To reduce the risk of heat illness, doctors recommend limiting outdoor activity during the hottest part of the day, taking frequent breaks in air conditioning, drinking water before feeling thirsty, and planning outdoor activities for the early morning or late evening whenever possible.
They also encourage checking on older adults, neighbors who live alone, and anyone with chronic medical conditions during prolonged stretches of dangerous heat.

SPRINGFIELD, Mo. (KY3) - Pavement temperatures reached nearly 120 degrees in open sunlight Monday, climbing to around 150 degrees during the late afternoon — conditions a local veterinarian says can pose serious risks to pets.
Dr. Philip Brown, a Springfield veterinarian at Animal Care Center, said extreme heat and humidity can make a routine walk dangerous for animals, especially certain breeds and pets with underlying health issues.
Paw pad burns
“When it’s hot enough to fry an egg on cement or asphalt, you’re going to have their feet pads burning,” Brown said.
Brown said pet owners may not notice a burn right away because they often do not examine the bottoms of the paws. He said signs can show up later, including tenderness or limping the next day.
For first aid, Brown recommends cooling the paws immediately.
“The first thing to do is stick them in water. Stick them immediately in water,” he said.
Brown said shaded routes can reduce the risk, and owners can alternate between pavement and grass. Dog booties can help prevent burns, he said, but they can also stress dogs that are not used to wearing them.
Higher-risk animals
Brown said dogs with short noses — known as brachycephalic breeds — are more susceptible in extreme heat because they do not cool as efficiently.
“You would look at dogs with shorter noses like bulldogs, French bulldogs,” Brown said, adding that Shih Tzus and Lhasa Apsos are also in that category.
He said pets with long-haired coats can also overheat, and owners should be careful about shaving dogs too closely because of the risk of sunburn.
Brown said owners should be especially cautious with pets that are overweight or have medical problems such as heart disease.
“If they’ve already got a heart problem, you surely don’t want to run them around in the heat,” Brown said.
He added that excess weight is a common risk factor.
“We’re also talking about 75-80% of our animals being overweight,” Brown said. “They’re going to get hotter faster.”
Signs of heat exhaustion and heat stroke
Brown said owners should watch for early warning signs such as a pet slowing down on walks or “starting to drag,” as well as heavy panting and a dry tongue or dry, tacky gums.
Brown said heat illness can progress from heat exhaustion to heat stroke, which can lead to seizures. He said a normal rectal temperature for a dog is generally 100.5 to 102.5 degrees, and sustained temperatures above 104 can begin damaging internal organs.
He said heat stroke can cause vomiting and bloody diarrhea from dehydration and should be treated as a medical emergency.
Owners should avoid putting an overheated pet into ice-cold water, Brown said, because cooling should be gradual.
“You don’t want to put them in ice-cold water. You want to put them in tepid water,” he said.
Brown said a cooling step owners can try while seeking help is to place a cold pack — even a bag of frozen vegetables or crushed ice — under the armpits or in the groin area, where major blood vessels can help circulate cooling through the body.
Water intake
Brown said access to fresh water is one of the most important factors in keeping pets safe during extreme heat, including for dogs kept outdoors.
“Dogs should have water access 24-7,” Brown said.
He offered a general guideline for daily intake.
“One ounce per pound — a 10-pound dog needs 10 ounces, a 50-pound dog needs 50 ounces,” Brown said.
Brown said canned food can help increase moisture intake because it contains more water than dry kibble, and some owners may need to add water to food for pets that are not strong drinkers.
He said owners should be careful with outside dogs on chains to make sure water bowls are not tipped over, which he said is when “the biggest problems occur.”
Indoor pets and cats
Brown said extreme heat can also be dangerous for indoor pets such as rabbits and guinea pigs, especially if they are kept in outdoor hutches.
He said owners can freeze a plastic bottle of water overnight and place it in a hutch or enclosure so the animal has a cooler surface to lie against as it melts, and a fan can also help.
For cats, Brown said overheating can happen when they sleep in a sunny window or become overactive while playing indoors. He said some cats drink more when water is moving, such as from a pet fountain or dripping tap, and owners should make sure cats have reliable access to water.
When to call a veterinarian
Brown said owners who suspect a pet is overheating — especially if symptoms persist or worsen — should contact a veterinarian.
“Always, always, always call your veterinarian,” he said. “They’re here to help you.”

Predicting heavy rains and thunderstorms, MET Office has issued a Yellow Alert for Huvadhu Atoll (Gaafu Alif, Gaafu Dhaalu atolls).
The Yellow Alert is issued from Gaafu Alif Atoll to Gaafu Dhaalu atoll from 1:15pm to 4pm today.
Northern and southern atolls of Maldives have been experiencing rainy weather over the past days. Although rainfall is comparatively low in the central atolls, winds remain strong.
According to the Maldivian Nakaiy Calendar, today marks the second day of Miaheli, the fifth nakaiy of Hulhan'gu Moosun (Southwest Monsoon).
Each 'nakaiy' lasts thirteen to fourteen days, with each having a distinct predictable weather pattern.
Miaheli nakaiy brings strong westerly winds and rough seas making sea travel risky.
With the advent of the Hulhan'gu monsoon, the country generally sees the strongest adverse weather patterns in June and July each year.
